title: Whole-Service Observability — detailed demonstration console
status: Delivery runbooks for the IIC Hybrid Orders demos, written to the design of record (lab/design/HYBRID-APPLICATION-HEALTH-DESIGN.md).

demos.title: Prove each evidence route
demos.objective: Slide 16. Prove, route by route, that evidence from the Arc-connected AWS machines and from the IIC order stages reaches the workspace: which DCR is associated with which machine, how fresh Heartbeat and Perf are, and that order stage records use the direct-ingestion route (dcr-cas26-requests-eus-01, no association). Collection is proven, not assumed from Arc registration.
prerequisites: PowerShell 7 from the repository root on the presenter jump, Azure CLI signed in to the CAS26 tenant with the log-analytics and resource-graph extensions installed during preparation, never on stage.
Copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json (gitignored) and fill every identifier with a verified value. Run the context loader with -Offline first, then without it.

Read access only is needed for every read-only step: Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, Reader on the monitoring RG and the AWS connector RG. No step changes an Azure or AWS resource except the application-level worker mode in M03.
Rehearse steps 2 and 3 within 24 hours of delivery and note which machines are associated and fresh; the numbers change as the AWS estate changes.

Know the expected machine list: the six IIC EC2 machines in the connector RG, production and development web, API and data tiers (iic-cas26-prd-web-01, iic-cas26-prd-api-01, iic-cas26-prd-data-01, iic-cas26-dev-web-01, iic-cas26-dev-api-01, iic-cas26-dev-data-01). iic-cas26-prd-api-01 hosts the AWS fulfillment worker. Any other Arc machine in that RG is outside the service scope.
demos.reset: Read-only; nothing to reset. Close the query tabs so the next demo starts from the workbook.
demos.fallback: If a query or the portal is slow, show the captured result from rehearsal (association list, freshness table, DCR show output, and src/fixtures/order-baseline.jsonl for the stage-record shape), say it is the rehearsal capture and name the step it stands in for.
demos.wait: Heartbeat arrives about once a minute and Perf at the DCR sample rate; ingestion adds a few minutes. Do not re-run a query more than once while waiting; read the timestamp instead.

steps.title: Select the machines and the time window
steps.body: Load the demo context and list the Arc-connected EC2 machines in the connector-created AWS resource group with Resource Graph. This fixes the scope: the machines we expect evidence from, their exact resource IDs and their connection state. The time window for every later query is the last 30 minutes.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
$arg = "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.hybridcompute/machines' | where resourceGroup =~ '$($Demo.AwsResourceGroup)' | project name, status=tostring(properties.status), os=tostring(properties.osName), id"
$machines = az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.WorkloadSubscriptionId -q $arg --first 50 -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$machines.data | Format-Table name, status, os -AutoSize
steps.expected: The six IIC EC2 machines with status Connected and their resource IDs. That is the expected source list; Connected proves Arc management, not that any evidence arrives. Any other machine in the RG is outside the service scope: name it and leave it out.
steps.troubleshooting: No rows: wrong subscription or RG name (the connector RG is lower case, aws_<AccountId>). A machine missing from the list: note it and carry on; do not widen the scope to other RGs.
steps.speaker: Start from scope, not from a dashboard. These IDs are the only machines we will accept evidence from in the next steps; Arc Connected is a management fact, not a telemetry fact.
steps.attendee: List the exact resources you expect evidence from before you query any evidence.

steps.title: Confirm each DCR association
steps.body: For every machine, list its data collection rule associations. An association is what binds a machine to a rule; without it AMA collects nothing for that rule, however healthy the agent is.
steps.expected: Each of the six machines lists dcr-tplabs-cas26-linux-eus-01. A machine with an empty Rules column would have no collection route, and that is the first thing to fix, before any query.
steps.troubleshooting: An authorization error means the identity lacks read on the Arc resource; do not switch identities on stage. An empty list for every machine usually means the wrong subscription context.
steps.speaker: The association is the wiring between machine and rule. We check it per machine, because a single missing association looks exactly like a quiet machine in every chart.
steps.attendee: Check the DCR association per machine; an installed agent without an association sends nothing for that rule.

steps.title: Query Heartbeat and Perf freshness for the Arc-connected AWS machines
steps.body: Run the freshness query scoped to the connector RG. It reports, per machine, the last Heartbeat and the last Perf sample against an expected maximum age. Heartbeat proves the agent can reach the workspace; Perf proves the DCR's counters flow.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/evidence-freshness.kql" -Raw).Replace('<AWS_RESOURCE_GROUP>', $Demo.AwsResourceGroup)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Rows 'Heartbeat / <machine>' and 'Perf / <machine>' with AgeMin inside ExpectedMaxAgeMin (Fresh) for each of the six machines, and 'Stage / <component> / <stage>' rows for the order records. A machine from step 1 that is missing here would be silent: that is a finding, not a healthy machine.
steps.troubleshooting: No rows at all: check the workspace GUID and the RG placeholder. Stale rows: check the machine's AMA extension state and the association from step 2. The stage-record route is examined on its own in step 4.
steps.speaker: Freshness is two numbers: when the last row arrived and how old it may be. A machine that is not in the result is the most important row, because silence is the failure mode dashboards hide.
steps.attendee: Compare the machines that report with the machines you expect; the missing ones are the finding.

steps.title: Check the stage-record route into Cas26Service_CL
steps.body: Order stage records do not come from an agent. The coordinator and workers send them through the Logs Ingestion API to the direct-ingestion DCR dcr-cas26-requests-eus-01, which has a logs-ingestion endpoint of its own and no association. Show the DCR, confirm it has no associations, then read the table schema.
steps.code:
az monitor data-collection rule show --ids $Demo.RequestsDcrResourceId --query "{name:name, kind:kind, endpoint:endpoints.logsIngestion, immutableId:immutableId, streams:keys(streamDeclarations), destination:dataFlows[0].outputStream}" -o json
az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com$($Demo.RequestsDcrResourceId)/associations?api-version=2022-06-01" --query "length(value)"
$q = 'Cas26Service_CL | getschema | project ColumnName, ColumnType'
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: kind Direct, a logs-ingestion endpoint, one custom stream flowing to Custom-Cas26Service_CL, and 0 associations. The schema lists the contract columns: CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Customer, Environment, Cloud, Origin, Component, Stage, Success, DurationMs, DemoTag, FailureMode and Computer next to TimeGenerated.
steps.troubleshooting: A Direct DCR with an association is a configuration mistake to record, not to fix on stage. A missing contract column is a schema defect: name it, and show src/fixtures/order-baseline.jsonl for the shape the queries expect.
steps.speaker: Two different routes land in one workspace. Agents need an association; the application's stage records use a direct DCR with its own endpoint and no association. The schema shows the contract columns every later query relies on.
steps.attendee: Application records sent through the Logs Ingestion API use a direct DCR endpoint; they do not need a DCR association.

steps.title: Verify freshness and identity
steps.body: Close the loop on identity: which Azure identity ran these queries, and does every Heartbeat row carry the exact Arc resource ID from step 1 rather than just a computer name? Then check the last stage record in Cas26Service_CL.
steps.code:
az account show --query "{user:user.name, tenant:tenantId, subscription:id}" -o table
$ids = @($machines.data.id | ForEach-Object { "'$($_.ToLower())'" }) -join ','
if (-not $ids) { throw 'No machines from step 1: fix the scope before checking identity.' }
$q = "Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(30m) | summarize LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by _ResourceId=tolower(_ResourceId) | extend Expected = _ResourceId in ($ids)"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$q = 'Cas26Service_CL | summarize LastRow=max(TimeGenerated), Rows=count()'
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: The presenter identity in the CAS26 tenant; Heartbeat rows whose _ResourceId matches an expected machine (Expected=true), and any row with Expected=false is evidence from outside the intended scope. Cas26Service_CL shows a last row from the latest orders, a few minutes old at most.
steps.troubleshooting: The guard stops the step: step 1 returned no machines, so fix the scope first rather than running an empty in (). Rows with Expected=false: another machine writes to this workspace; name it and exclude it from the service view. An old last row in Cas26Service_CL: no orders have been placed recently; check the order stream before M02.
steps.speaker: Evidence is only useful if we know whose it is. Resource IDs, not names, tie a row to a machine; and the identity running the query decides what we can see.
steps.attendee: Tie every evidence row to a resource ID and know which identity read it.

demos.title: Place a baseline order and read the service view
demos.objective: Slides 20 (stage 1 of 2) and 21 (stage 2 of 2). Stage 1 places demo-tagged IIC orders through Front Door (the first is the baseline order we follow) and reads the baseline's stage records by correlation ID, so failure and recovery have a comparison point. Stage 2 reads the service view in the fixed order taught on slide 19 (customer outcome, overall health, components and dependencies, evidence freshness, drill-down with owners) and checks that the view agrees with the raw stage records and that both portal origins are healthy.
prerequisites: PowerShell 7 from the repository root on the presenter jump, Azure CLI signed in to the CAS26 tenant with the log-analytics and resource-graph extensions installed during preparation, never on stage.
Copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json (gitignored) and fill every identifier with a verified value. Run the context loader with -Offline first, then without it.

Read access only is needed for every read-only step: Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, Reader on the monitoring RG and the AWS connector RG. No step changes an Azure or AWS resource except the application-level worker mode in M03.
Before delivery confirm: both portal origins healthy in Front Door, both workers in Healthy mode, and ServiceUrl, FrontDoorProfileResourceId and WorkbookResourceId recorded in demo.local.json.
Open the workbook "CAS26 service operations" in a browser tab before the session, set to the last 30 minutes, light theme.
demos.reset: Nothing to reset: the baseline orders are normal demo-tagged orders. Keep them in $baselineOrders, and the first one in $baseline, for M03 and M04.
demos.fallback: If the order client, a query or the workbook is slow, replay src/fixtures/order-baseline.jsonl with scripts/Show-Cas26Fixture.ps1 or show the rehearsal screenshot of the view, say it is the rehearsal capture and name the step; then return to the live view when it has refreshed.
demos.wait: The order result returns to the client before its stage rows are queryable; allow a few minutes of ingestion before querying and state the gap out loud. Workbook tiles refresh on their own schedule.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 20): check the starting state
steps.body: Load the context and confirm the starting state: the AWS worker must be in Healthy mode before the baseline. The dry run reads the worker's mode over SSM without changing it.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
pwsh ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Healthy -InstanceId $Demo.AwsWorkerInstanceId -AwsRegion $Demo.AwsRegion -DryRun
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Worker state could not be read; check the AWS CLI sign-in on the jump.' }
steps.expected: A DRY RUN line showing the AWS worker is already Healthy; no change is needed.
steps.troubleshooting: DryRun fails: the AWS CLI or SSM path from the jump is not signed in; fix it before continuing. PreviousMode other than Healthy: a fault was left on; reset it with -Mode Healthy before the baseline.
steps.speaker: A baseline only means something if we know the starting state. The dry run reads the worker's mode without changing it.
steps.attendee: Record the starting state before taking a baseline.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 20): place demo-tagged orders through Front Door
steps.body: Place three orders with the demo tag through the public Front Door endpoint, two seconds apart, so the five-minute window holds the three samples the health signals need. The first is the baseline order we follow: record its correlation ID, order number, serving origin (Azure or AWS), status and elapsed time. The correlation ID is the key for everything that follows; the order number is for people.
steps.code:
$baselineOrders = @(& ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 -BaseUri $Demo.ServiceUrl -DemoTag -Count 3 -IntervalSeconds 2 -JsonLinesPath $S/evidence/local/m02-baseline.jsonl)
$baseline = $baselineOrders[0]
$baselineOrders | Select-Object CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Origin, Status, ElapsedMs, FailureMode
$baseline.Stages | Format-Table Cloud, Component, Stage, Success, DurationMs
steps.expected: Three results with Status Completed and new CorrelationIds, served by the Azure or AWS origin; the baseline order's stages from Azure, OnPrem and AWS are all successful.
steps.troubleshooting: Status Failed with a FailureMode: a fault mode is still active; reset and re-place. TimedOut: note the time and find the order by time window in step 3. A contract error from the script means the endpoint's response shape changed; stop and show the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: These are application writes, three demo-tagged orders, nothing else. The client sees the answer first; the evidence follows through ingestion.
steps.attendee: One correlation ID is the thread that ties a customer order to every stage in every cloud.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 20): read the order's stage records
steps.body: Query the workspace for this correlation ID. The rows are the evidence of what happened, independent of what the client was told.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/order-journey.kql" -Raw).Replace('<CORRELATION_ID>', $baseline.CorrelationId)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Seven rows in time order: Coordinator Accepted (with Origin), Transport Dispatched, OnPremWorker and AwsWorker Started and Completed, then Coordinator Completed with Success true.
steps.troubleshooting: No rows yet: ingestion delay; wait once, then re-run. Fewer rows: a stage did not report; that is the finding. If ingestion is slow on stage, show src/fixtures/order-baseline.jsonl as the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Read the rows as a timeline across three clouds. The last row, Coordinator Completed, is the customer outcome; the others explain it.
steps.attendee: Query stage records by the correlation ID, never by the display order number.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 20): judge the order as the service sees it
steps.body: Run the service-outcome query. It summarizes by correlation ID first, so each order counts once, and marks it Completed only when the coordinator wrote its Completed row. Confirm the baseline is Completed inside the target.
steps.code:
$q = Get-Content "$S/src/queries/service-outcome.kql" -Raw
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: The three baseline orders, each listed once with Outcome Completed, Clouds [Azure, OnPrem, AWS] and ElapsedMs inside the order target.
steps.troubleshooting: The order appears as Unresolved: the coordinator's Completed row has not arrived yet or was never written. Several rows for one order means the query was edited to skip the summarize-by-CorrelationId step.
steps.speaker: Counting rows would count stages, not customers. Summarizing by correlation ID first turns seven stage rows into one customer outcome.
steps.attendee: Summarize by correlation ID before you count successes.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 21): open the service view and read it in the fixed order
steps.body: Open the workbook and read it in the order slide 19 taught: 1 the customer outcome (order success, latency, last good order), 2 overall health (state, freshness, affected commitment), 3 components and dependencies (portal origins, coordinator, both workers), 4 evidence freshness (latest timestamps, late sources), 5 drill-down (correlation ID, stage timeline and owners). Say what each panel answers before looking at its colour.
steps.code:
az resource show --ids $Demo.WorkbookResourceId --query "{name:properties.displayName, updated:properties.timeModified, source:properties.sourceId}" -o table
# Portal: Azure portal > Monitor > Workbooks > CAS26 service operations (RG rg-tplabs-cas26-mon-eus-01), time range last 30 minutes
steps.expected: The workbook is the one named and recently modified, and its panels follow that order: the baseline orders in the customer-outcome panel, overall health Healthy, both origins, the coordinator and both workers green, every source fresh, and the drill-down ready for a correlation ID.
steps.troubleshooting: The workbook does not open: check Reader on the monitoring RG. A panel reports a query error: name the panel and read the same answer from the raw query in step 4.
steps.speaker: A service view is read in a fixed order so that a green component never distracts from a failed customer outcome. The workbook drills down; the Health Model, later, evaluates.
steps.attendee: Read a service view from customer outcome to overall health to components to freshness to drill-down.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 21): open the baseline order's stages in the view
steps.body: In the correlation panel, select the baseline order's correlation ID and compare what the view shows with the raw rows from step 3. The view is only trustworthy if it agrees with the rows.
steps.code:
$baseline.CorrelationId | Set-Clipboard
# Portal: paste into the workbook's correlation panel filter and compare stage by stage with the query result from step 3
steps.expected: The view shows the same seven stages, the same clouds and the same success values as the raw query. Any difference is a view defect to record.
steps.troubleshooting: The panel shows a different stage count: its time range or filter differs from the query; align them before calling it a view defect, and record any difference that remains.
steps.speaker: The view is a lens on the evidence, not the evidence. We prove it by matching one order's rows exactly.
steps.attendee: Check one known order in the view against the raw records before trusting the view.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 21): check both portal origins
steps.body: The portal is redundant: Front Door serves it from Azure Container Apps and from the AWS ALB/EKS origin. Read the origin health metric and which origins served recent orders. One healthy origin keeps customers in; two is the design target.
steps.code:
az monitor metrics list --resource $Demo.FrontDoorProfileResourceId --metric OriginHealthPercentage --interval PT5M --offset 1h --aggregation Average -o table
$q = "Cas26Service_CL | where TimeGenerated > ago(30m) | where Component == 'Coordinator' and Stage == 'Accepted' | summarize Orders=dcount(CorrelationId), Last=max(TimeGenerated) by Origin"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Origin health near 100 percent, and recent orders served by both Azure and AWS origins. One origin at 0 would make the portal Degraded, not down.
steps.troubleshooting: The metric is empty: check FrontDoorProfileResourceId and the time range. Only one origin appears in the orders: routing weights or a small sample; place a few more orders with -Count 3 if time allows.
steps.speaker: Portal availability and order completion are different commitments. Two origins behind Front Door protect the first; the second depends on both workers.
steps.attendee: Treat redundant origins as one commitment with a degraded state, not as two separate alarms.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 21): note freshness and owners
steps.body: Finish the reading with freshness and ownership: when did each source and each stage last report, and who owns each component? The owner is what turns a red tile into an action.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/evidence-freshness.kql" -Raw).Replace('<AWS_RESOURCE_GROUP>', $Demo.AwsResourceGroup)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
# Owners (from the lab design): Coordinator and Transport - Azure application team; OnPremWorker - private cloud team; AwsWorker - AWS workload team; telemetry routes - monitoring team
steps.expected: Every stage and every source Fresh, and a named owner for each component the view shows.
steps.troubleshooting: Stale stage rows while the order was just placed: ingestion delay; re-read the timestamp, do not re-run in a loop. A component with no owner is a gap to record in the evidence notes.
steps.speaker: Freshness tells us whether we may believe the colours; owners tell us who acts. Both belong in the view, not in someone's head.
steps.attendee: Every panel in a service view needs a freshness time and an owner.

demos.title: Follow the controlled fault, then prove recovery with a fresh order
demos.objective: Slides 23 (stage 1: the marvin fault) and 34 (stage 2: recovery). Stage 1 sets the AWS worker to Fail (fault marvin) for demo-tagged orders only, places fresh orders and follows them: the AWS fulfillment stage fails, the orders fail, and the machines stay healthy. In IIC the AWS worker is inside the order path, so its fault is the cause and the evidence proves it. Stage 2 resets the worker to Healthy, places new orders with new correlation IDs and watches the model and alert catch up: recovery is a new observation, not a recycled screenshot.
prerequisites: PowerShell 7 from the repository root on the presenter jump, Azure CLI signed in to the CAS26 tenant with the log-analytics and resource-graph extensions installed during preparation, never on stage.
Copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json (gitignored) and fill every identifier with a verified value. Run the context loader with -Offline first, then without it.

Read access only is needed for every read-only step: Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, Reader on the monitoring RG and the AWS connector RG. No step changes an Azure or AWS resource except the application-level worker mode in M03.

Before delivery confirm: the AWS worker on iic-cas26-prd-api-01 (AwsWorkerInstanceId) is in Healthy mode and reads /var/lib/cas26/worker-state.json on every message; the AWS CLI on the jump is signed in with ssm:SendCommand and ssm:GetCommandInvocation on that instance only; the M02 baseline orders are in $baselineOrders and $baseline.

Only the AWS worker's application mode changes. Never stop the service, the instance, EKS, the ALB, the Arc agent or any network path. MaxMinutes 15 is the automatic backstop; the reset in stage 2 is the planned end.
Decide the presenter's stop condition before starting: if the fault command reports anything other than PreviousMode Healthy and Mode Fail, stop and reset.
demos.reset: pwsh ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Healthy -InstanceId $Demo.AwsWorkerInstanceId -AwsRegion $Demo.AwsRegion, then place a new demo-tagged order and confirm Status Completed. As a backstop the worker stops applying the fault at expires_at (15 minutes). A successful SSM command alone is not recovery evidence.
demos.fallback: If ingestion, the model or the alert list is slow, replay the rehearsal captures with scripts/Show-Cas26Fixture.ps1: src/fixtures/order-marvin.jsonl and src/fixtures/heartbeat-aws-worker.jsonl for stage 1, src/fixtures/order-recovery.jsonl for stage 2. Say they are the captured results from rehearsal, name the step, and give the expected model and alert times from the timing notes.
demos.wait: The failed orders return in seconds; their rows need ingestion time; the Health Model re-evaluates on its refresh interval (PT1M) over its window (PT5M); the service-failure alert evaluates every 5 minutes over a 5-minute window, fires on the first evaluation that sees at least three orders with half or more failed, and, being stateful, resolves after three consecutive evaluations without the condition, about 15 minutes after the last failing window. Stage 2 happens later in the deck, which is the time the model and alert need.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 23): preview the fault on the AWS worker
steps.body: Load the context and run the fault command as a dry run. It reads the worker's current state over SSM and prints the file it would write, without writing it. Confirm the target is the AWS worker and its current mode is Healthy.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
pwsh ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Fail -InstanceId $Demo.AwsWorkerInstanceId -AwsRegion $Demo.AwsRegion -MaxMinutes 15 -DryRun
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Fault preview failed; no change is authorized.' }
steps.expected: DRY RUN line naming the instance and /var/lib/cas26/worker-state.json, current mode Healthy, proposed mode Fail with faultName marvin and expires_at 15 minutes ahead.
steps.troubleshooting: Preview fails: SSM or AWS identity problem; do not attempt the change; fix the AWS sign-in and preview again, or show the rehearsal capture. The file is reported as not owned by CAS26: stop; something else owns that path.
steps.speaker: A fault is only safe if it is previewed, bounded and reversible. The dry run shows all three before anything changes.
steps.attendee: Preview every fault command and confirm its target and expiry before applying it.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 23): set the AWS worker to Fail (marvin) for demo-tagged orders
steps.body: Apply the fault. The worker now returns a deliberate failed stage result for demo-tagged orders only; untagged orders are unaffected, and the service, instance and network are untouched.
steps.code:
pwsh ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Fail -InstanceId $Demo.AwsWorkerInstanceId -AwsRegion $Demo.AwsRegion -MaxMinutes 15
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Fault change failed; reset with -Mode Healthy before continuing.' }
steps.expected: Output with Mode Fail, FaultName marvin, PreviousMode Healthy, Changed True and an ExpiresAt time.
steps.troubleshooting: Any error: run the reset command immediately and show the rehearsal capture. Do not retry the fault more than once on stage.
steps.speaker: This is the only change in the session: one file on one worker, application-level, with an expiry. Everything else we do is observation.
steps.attendee: Fault the application behaviour you own, not the infrastructure other people depend on.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 23): place fresh demo-tagged orders
steps.body: Place three new orders with the demo tag, two seconds apart: the service-failure alert only judges a window with at least three orders. The client result already tells the story: each order failed and the failure mode is marvin. Keep the correlation IDs.
steps.code:
$failed = @(& ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 -BaseUri $Demo.ServiceUrl -DemoTag -Count 3 -IntervalSeconds 2 -JsonLinesPath $S/evidence/local/m03-marvin.jsonl)
$failed | Select-Object CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Origin, Status, ElapsedMs, FailureMode
$failed[0].Stages | Format-Table Cloud, Component, Stage, Success, DurationMs
steps.expected: Three results with Status Failed, FailureMode marvin and new CorrelationIds; in each, the AwsWorker stage has Success False while the OnPremWorker stage succeeded.
steps.troubleshooting: Status Completed: the orders were not demo-tagged or the worker did not read the new state; check the file with a DryRun. The portal itself still loads: that is part of the point.
steps.speaker: The portal answered, Front Door routed, the coordinator accepted: the customer still did not get an order. Front-end availability is not order completion.
steps.attendee: A working portal and a completed order are different commitments.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 23): read the failed order's stages
steps.body: Query the stage records for the first failed order and read them as a timeline. Then run the service outcome to see how the service counts the orders.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/order-journey.kql" -Raw).Replace('<CORRELATION_ID>', $failed[0].CorrelationId)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$q = Get-Content "$S/src/queries/service-outcome.kql" -Raw
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: AwsWorker Failed with Success false and FailureMode marvin; OnPremWorker Completed; Coordinator Failed. In the outcome list the three marvin orders are Failed with FailedComponents [AwsWorker, Coordinator], next to the Completed baseline orders.
steps.troubleshooting: No AwsWorker row at all: the worker did not report, which is a different fault (missing evidence, later Unknown); say so rather than calling it marvin. If ingestion is slow, show src/fixtures/order-marvin.jsonl as the rehearsal capture and name the step.
steps.speaker: The evidence points at one stage in one cloud, with the fault name on the row. Investigation starts from the customer outcome and walks back to the first failed stage.
steps.attendee: Walk back from the failed outcome to the first failed stage; the fault name on the row confirms a controlled fault.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 23): see the order fail while the machines stay healthy
steps.body: Check the AWS worker machine's Heartbeat and CPU for the same window, then glance at the Health Model. The machine is fine; the order is not. Infrastructure health cannot stand in for the customer outcome.
steps.code:
$q = "Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | where _ResourceId =~ '$($Demo.AwsWorkerArcResourceId)' | summarize LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Beats=count() by Computer"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$q = "Perf | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | where _ResourceId =~ '$($Demo.AwsWorkerArcResourceId)' | where CounterName == '% Processor Time' and InstanceName == '_Total' | summarize AvgCpu=avg(CounterValue), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated)"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
# Portal: Monitor > Health models > hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01 > graph
steps.expected: Heartbeat for iic-cas26-prd-api-01 fresh (about one beat a minute) and total CPU unremarkable during the fault. In the model graph, after its window, the Arc-enabled AWS worker is Unhealthy on its stage evidence, AWS fulfillment and pricing is Unhealthy, Customers can complete an order is Unhealthy and the service root follows; the portal commitment stays Healthy.
steps.troubleshooting: Heartbeat missing: that is a real monitoring problem on the machine, not part of this fault; name it. If the query is slow, src/fixtures/heartbeat-aws-worker.jsonl is the rehearsal capture of the machine staying fresh through the fault window. The model has not changed yet: its window is five minutes; come back to it in M04.
steps.speaker: This is the SCOM lesson in one screen: every host green, the service red. Health has to be defined by the customer commitment, with the machines as evidence.
steps.attendee: Machine health is supporting evidence; the customer outcome is the signal.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 34): set the AWS worker back to Healthy
steps.body: After the response teaching, reset the worker. The command reads the current state first, so the output shows it moved from Fail back to Healthy.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
pwsh ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Healthy -InstanceId $Demo.AwsWorkerInstanceId -AwsRegion $Demo.AwsRegion
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'RECOVERY FAILED: restore the AWS worker before proceeding.' }
steps.expected: Mode Healthy, PreviousMode Fail, Changed True (the worker, not the script, applies the expiry).
steps.troubleshooting: Failure: retry once; if it still fails, the worker stops applying the fault at expires_at by itself; say so and show the recovery capture. Never leave the session with the worker in Fail.
steps.speaker: The management command succeeding tells us the file changed. It does not tell us a customer can order again; only a new order can.
steps.attendee: A successful reset command is not recovery evidence.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 34): place new demo-tagged orders
steps.body: Place three fresh orders, two seconds apart. Each must have a new correlation ID; reusing the baseline would prove nothing about now. Three orders also give the model and the alert a full window of good samples.
steps.code:
$recovered = @(& ./sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos/scripts/Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 -BaseUri $Demo.ServiceUrl -DemoTag -Count 3 -IntervalSeconds 2 -JsonLinesPath $S/evidence/local/m03-recovery.jsonl)
$recovered | Select-Object CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Origin, Status, ElapsedMs, FailureMode
$used = @($baselineOrders.CorrelationId) + @($failed.CorrelationId)
if (@($recovered.CorrelationId | Where-Object { $_ -in $used }).Count) { throw 'Not a new order.' }
steps.expected: Three results with Status Completed, empty FailureMode, and CorrelationIds different from every baseline and failed order.
steps.troubleshooting: Still Failed with marvin: the worker has not re-read the state; check with a DryRun and wait one message. Failed with another mode: another fault is active; stop and investigate before claiming recovery.
steps.speaker: Recovery is a new observation of the same commitment: a new order, placed now, that completes.
steps.attendee: Prove recovery with a new transaction, not with the last good screenshot.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 34): confirm every stage and the order completed
steps.body: Read the first recovery order's stages and the service outcome. The list now shows the baseline orders Completed, the marvin orders Failed and the recovery orders Completed, in that order of time.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/order-journey.kql" -Raw).Replace('<CORRELATION_ID>', $recovered[0].CorrelationId)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/service-outcome.kql" -Raw).Replace('ago(window)', 'ago(2h)')
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Seven successful stage rows for the recovery order ending in Coordinator Completed; the outcome list shows Completed, Failed, Completed across the three groups of orders.
steps.troubleshooting: Rows missing: ingestion delay; wait once. If the rows are slow to arrive, show src/fixtures/order-recovery.jsonl as the rehearsal capture and name the step.
steps.speaker: Three groups of orders, each with its own correlation IDs, one story: normal, controlled failure, recovered. The evidence carries the timeline.
steps.attendee: Keep the failed and the recovered order side by side; the comparison is the proof.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 34): watch the model and the alert catch up
steps.body: Open the Health Model graph and the alert list. The model returns to Healthy once its five-minute window holds enough good samples; the alert resolves on its own evaluation schedule. Record both times against the order times.
steps.code:
$arg = "alertsmanagementresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.alertsmanagement/alerts' | where todatetime(properties.essentials.startDateTime) > ago(2h) | project name=tostring(properties.essentials.alertRule), condition=tostring(properties.essentials.monitorCondition), state=tostring(properties.essentials.alertState), started=todatetime(properties.essentials.startDateTime), changed=todatetime(properties.essentials.lastModifiedDateTime)"
az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.MonitoringSubscriptionId -q $arg -o table
# Portal: Monitor > Health models > hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01 > graph and history
steps.expected: The service-failure alert (CAS26 service: request failures) fired on the first 5-minute evaluation after the three marvin orders (at least three orders, half or more failed) and shows Resolved about 15 minutes after the last failing window, because a stateful log search alert resolves only after three consecutive evaluations without the condition. The model's AWS worker, AWS fulfillment and Customers can complete an order entities return to Healthy once the window holds the three recovery orders and no failures. Each state change has a time later than the order that caused it.
steps.troubleshooting: The alert still shows Fired: it resolves after three clean 5-minute evaluations; read its last-modified time instead of refreshing. The model reads Unknown: no orders in its five-minute window, which is the correct reading of silence; place one more demo-tagged order if time allows.
steps.speaker: Four clocks: the order, ingestion, model evaluation and alert evaluation. Recovery is complete when the customer order succeeds; the model and alert confirm it later, and we can say how much later.
steps.attendee: Know how long your model and alerts lag behind the customer outcome.

demos.title: Inspect the model configuration, then explain the current state from evidence
demos.objective: Slides 29 (stage 1 of 2) and 30 (stage 2 of 2). Stage 1 opens the IIC health model and reads its configuration in the order stage 2 uses: entities, relationship direction, one signal's query, window and thresholds, aggregation and missing-data behaviour. Stage 2 explains state from evidence: current stage records and timestamps, the signal's value against its rule, aggregation to the commitment and propagation to the service, from Healthy at baseline to AWS fulfillment Unhealthy during the marvin fault. If evidence is stale, the honest state is Unknown.
prerequisites: PowerShell 7 from the repository root on the presenter jump, Azure CLI signed in to the CAS26 tenant with the log-analytics and resource-graph extensions installed during preparation, never on stage.
Copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json (gitignored) and fill every identifier with a verified value. Run the context loader with -Offline first, then without it.

Read access only is needed for every read-only step: Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, Reader on the monitoring RG and the AWS connector RG. No step changes an Azure or AWS resource except the application-level worker mode in M03.

Health Models is a preview service; the REST calls use api-version 2026-09-01-preview (HealthModelApiVersion in demo.local.json). If that version is not served in Central US, use the version the resource was deployed with (see shared/foundation/terraform/modules/health/main.tf).
Reader on rg-tplabs-cas26-mon-eus-01 is enough for every step; no model change is made on stage.
Have the IIC model tree from lab/design/HYBRID-APPLICATION-HEALTH-DESIGN.md open in a second tab as the reference drawing.
demos.reset: Read-only; nothing to reset. Close the model blade without saving any edit.
demos.fallback: If the portal or the REST calls are slow, show the rehearsal JSON of the model, entities and relationships and the rehearsal screenshot of the signal history, say they are the rehearsal capture and name the step. For stage 2, src/fixtures/order-baseline.jsonl shows the stage records a Healthy window is made of.
demos.wait: Model state updates on each signal's refresh interval (PT1M) over its window (PT5M). Do not refresh repeatedly; read the evaluation time shown with each state.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 29): open the IIC health model
steps.body: Open the model in the portal and read its resource properties from ARM. Note the region (Central US, because East US is not a supported preview region), the identity it uses to read evidence, and the provisioning state.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
$hm = "https://management.azure.com$($Demo.HealthModelResourceId)"; $api = "api-version=$($Demo.HealthModelApiVersion)"
az rest --method get --url "$($hm)?$api" --query "{name:name, location:location, state:properties.provisioningState, identity:identity.type}" -o table
# Portal: Azure portal > Monitor > Health models > hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01
steps.expected: hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01 in centralus, Succeeded, with a user-assigned identity. The portal graph opens.
steps.troubleshooting: An API-version error: use the version in the prerequisites and note it. Not found: wrong subscription in HealthModelResourceId.
steps.speaker: The model is an Azure resource with its own identity; that identity, not the presenter, reads the evidence. That matters when a signal goes Unknown for lack of permission.
steps.attendee: A health model reads evidence with its own identity; check it has access to every source.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 29): read the entities
steps.body: List the model's entities with their display names, impact and current health, and keep them for the next steps. Compare them with the IIC tree: the service, its three commitments, and the branches and components beneath each.
steps.code:
$entities = (az rest --method get --url "$hm/entities?$api" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json).value
$entities | Select-Object name, @{n='displayName';e={$_.properties.displayName}}, @{n='impact';e={$_.properties.impact}}, @{n='health';e={$_.properties.healthState}} | Format-Table -AutoSize
steps.expected: The root entity IIC Hybrid Orders; the three commitments Customers can open the portal, Customers can complete an order and Operators can observe the service; beneath them Global entry and protection, Cloud portal origins (Azure Container Apps origin, AWS ALB -> EKS origin), Azure request coordination (Function coordinator, Service Bus transport), On-premises order validation (the cas26-lnx01 workload VM and its SDN egress path), AWS fulfillment and pricing (the Arc-enabled AWS worker iic-cas26-prd-api-01), and Log Analytics ingestion and Azure Monitor workspace metrics.
steps.troubleshooting: No healthState column: the property name differs in this API version; read the state in the portal instead. Entities that differ from the tree: someone changed the model; read, do not fix.
steps.speaker: Entities are commitments and components, named in plain words. The tree on screen is the tree we drew: service, three commitments, then the parts each commitment needs.
steps.attendee: Name entities after commitments customers recognise, then add the components beneath them.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 29): read relationship direction
steps.body: List the relationships. Each one says a parent depends on a child, so the child's health propagates upward. Direction is what makes a worker fault reach the customer commitment.
steps.expected: Parent-to-child pairs from the root to each commitment, from each commitment to its branches, and from each branch to its components, for example Customers can complete an order -> AWS fulfillment and pricing -> Arc-enabled AWS worker. Azure request coordination, On-premises order validation and AWS fulfillment and pricing are all required children of Customers can complete an order.
steps.troubleshooting: Parent and child look reversed: read the portal graph's arrows before claiming a defect.
steps.speaker: Relationships point from what you promise to what it depends on. Get the direction wrong and a failed worker never reaches the customer outcome.
steps.attendee: Draw dependency direction from the commitment down to its components.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 29): open one signal's query, window and thresholds
steps.body: Open the Customers can complete an order entity and read its Log Analytics signals: the query text, the value column, the time grain (window), the refresh interval and the Degraded and Unhealthy rules.
steps.expected: request-failure-percent: FailurePercent over PT5M, refreshed PT1M, Degraded above 0, Unhealthy at or above 50, with a three-order minimum in the query. telemetry-coverage: Samples, Unhealthy below 3. The query text summarizes the stage rows by CorrelationId and counts an order Completed only on Coordinator / Completed / Success=true, the same rule as service-outcome.kql.
steps.troubleshooting: signalGroups is empty: the signals are defined elsewhere in this API version; open the entity's Signals tab in the portal instead.
steps.speaker: A colour is a rule applied to a number from a query over a window. Read all four before believing the colour, and check that the signal judges an order exactly as the service-outcome query does.
steps.attendee: For every signal, know its query, its window and its thresholds.

steps.title: Stage 1 (slide 29): check aggregation and missing-data behaviour
steps.body: Read how the commitment combines its children and what it does when evidence is missing: the dependency aggregation type and whether Unknown children are ignored. Then read the redundancy rule on the portal origins, and state what happens when a signal query returns no rows.
steps.code:
$order.properties.signalGroups.dependencies | Format-List aggregationType, ignoreUnknown
$origins = $entities | Where-Object { $_.properties.displayName -eq 'Cloud portal origins' }
$origins.properties.signalGroups.dependencies | Format-List
# A signal whose query returns no rows (no stage records in the window, or fewer than three resolved orders) has no value: the entity shows Unknown, not Healthy.
steps.expected: Customers can complete an order: aggregationType WorstOf and ignoreUnknown false, so the worst required child wins and an Unknown child is not ignored. Cloud portal origins: a redundancy rule, so one failed origin makes the portal Degraded and two make it Unhealthy. No valid samples means Unknown: the coverage query returns no row when the window has no stage records, and the failure query returns no row below three resolved orders.
steps.troubleshooting: Properties absent: the portal shows them under the entity's health aggregation settings.
steps.speaker: Missing evidence must never look like good news. WorstOf with Unknown not ignored is the conservative choice: silence makes the service Unknown rather than green.
steps.attendee: Configure missing data to produce Unknown, and decide explicitly how children aggregate.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 30): start from current stage records and timestamps
steps.body: Explain state from evidence, bottom up. First, what evidence exists right now for the signals to read: the last stage records per component and stage, with their age.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/evidence-freshness.kql" -Raw).Replace('<AWS_RESOURCE_GROUP>', $Demo.AwsResourceGroup)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Stage rows for every component and stage (Coordinator, Transport, OnPremWorker, AwsWorker) with LastSeen times from the M02 and M03 orders, including AwsWorker / Failed from the marvin orders, and Fresh Heartbeat and Perf rows for the six AWS machines.
steps.troubleshooting: Stage rows older than their expected age: no orders since M03, so the current window can only read Unknown; the signal history still explains the earlier states.
steps.speaker: State is only as current as its newest evidence. We read timestamps before we read colours.
steps.attendee: Check evidence age before interpreting any health state.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 30): evaluate the signal yourself
steps.body: Run the signal's own query in the workspace, first for the current window and then for the five minutes of the marvin orders, and compare each value with the rules. This is exactly what the model does each refresh; doing it by hand shows there is no magic.
steps.code:
$q = $signal.queryText
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$from = ([datetime]$failed[0].PlacedAtUtc).ToUniversalTime().AddMinutes(-1).ToString('o')
$qFault = $q.Replace('TimeGenerated > ago(5m)', "TimeGenerated between (datetime($from) .. 5m)")
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $qFault -o table
steps.expected: For the marvin window: FailurePercent at or above 50 (100 when only the three marvin orders are in it), which is Unhealthy. For the current window: a FailurePercent to compare with the rules (0 = Healthy, above 0 = Degraded, 50 or more = Unhealthy), or no row when fewer than three orders resolved in the last five minutes, which the model shows as Unknown.
steps.troubleshooting: $failed is not in this terminal: read PlacedAtUtc from evidence/local/m03-marvin.jsonl. The query errors: record it as a signal configuration defect; the model shows an error or Unknown for that signal.
steps.speaker: The model evaluates a query over a window against a rule. Running the query ourselves turns the colour into a number we can defend.
steps.attendee: Re-run a health signal's query by hand when a state surprises you.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 30): follow aggregation to the commitment and propagation to the service
steps.body: Read each entity's current state from the bottom up: worker, then the request flow, then the model root. Explain each state from the signal value and the aggregation rule, and say where the evidence stops.
steps.code:
az rest --method get --url "$hm/entities?$api" --query "value[].{name:name, displayName:properties.displayName, health:properties.healthState}" -o table
# Portal: model graph; select each entity and open its signal history for the last hour
steps.expected: In the signal history for the last hour: Healthy through the baseline window; during the marvin window the Arc-enabled AWS worker is Unhealthy on its stage evidence while its heartbeat stays fresh, AWS fulfillment and pricing is Unhealthy, Customers can complete an order is Unhealthy and IIC Hybrid Orders follows by WorstOf, while Customers can open the portal and Operators can observe the service stay Healthy. The current state matches the current window's signals, and every parent matches its worst required child.
steps.troubleshooting: An entity shows Healthy with no samples: a signal or rule is misconfigured; record it. If states lag the evidence, point at the refresh interval and window rather than refreshing.
steps.speaker: Propagation is arithmetic, not judgement: children's states combine by rule into the parent's. If we cannot explain a state from its evidence, we do not report it.
steps.attendee: Explain every state from its signal, window, rule and children, or report it as Unknown.

steps.title: Stage 2 (slide 30): state the limits
steps.body: Close with what the model can and cannot claim. Every branch of the IIC tree is bound, but each state is only as good as its window, its minimum samples and its freshest evidence. Name the limits, then show the baseline order's records to recall what a Healthy window is made of.
steps.code:
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/order-journey.kql" -Raw).Replace('<CORRELATION_ID>', $baseline.CorrelationId)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: A spoken limits statement: a five-minute window, a three-order minimum, a one-minute refresh, and no orders in the window reads Unknown, not Healthy; machine health is supporting evidence only. The baseline order's seven successful stage rows are on screen.
steps.troubleshooting: $baseline is not in this terminal: read the correlation ID from evidence/local/m02-baseline.jsonl. If time is short, say the limits in one sentence and move on.
steps.speaker: A health model is a claim about the service. Its limits are part of the claim: the window, the minimum samples, and the places where it can only say Unknown.
steps.attendee: Publish a health model's limits together with its states.

demos.title: Test evidence freshness and cost boundaries
demos.objective: Slide 38. Use the previous two slides' decision structure on real data: query the last timestamp per source and per stage, compare it with the expected cadence, run billable volume by table, then name one reduction and the diagnostic question it would lose.
prerequisites: PowerShell 7 from the repository root on the presenter jump, Azure CLI signed in to the CAS26 tenant with the log-analytics and resource-graph extensions installed during preparation, never on stage.
Copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json (gitignored) and fill every identifier with a verified value. Run the context loader with -Offline first, then without it.

Read access only is needed for every read-only step: Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, Reader on the monitoring RG and the AWS connector RG. No step changes an Azure or AWS resource except the application-level worker mode in M03.
The per-order cost step reads the last full day of stage records; run it once in rehearsal and keep the result under evidence/local/.
Prepare the decision record location: demos/evidence/local/m05-decision.md (gitignored).
demos.reset: Read-only; nothing to reset. No DCR, table plan or retention setting is changed on stage; a reduction is recorded as a decision, not applied.
demos.fallback: If a query is slow, show the rehearsal capture of the freshness and volume results (src/fixtures/usage-by-table.jsonl holds the volume result's shape), say it is the rehearsal capture and name the step. Quote cost figures only from a live query.
demos.wait: Usage rows are hourly aggregates and lag ingestion; use full days for volume. Freshness results are read once.

steps.title: Query the last timestamp per source and per stage
steps.body: Run the freshness query across the three routes: Heartbeat and Perf from each Arc-connected AWS machine, and each component and stage of the order records.
steps.code:
$S = './sessions/azure-monitor-hybrid-multicloud-observability/demos'
. $S/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath $S/config/demo.local.json
$q = (Get-Content "$S/src/queries/evidence-freshness.kql" -Raw).Replace('<AWS_RESOURCE_GROUP>', $Demo.AwsResourceGroup)
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: One row per source with LastSeen, AgeMin, ExpectedMaxAgeMin and Freshness: Heartbeat and Perf Fresh for the six AWS machines, and stage rows Fresh for each component and stage written by the recent orders.
steps.troubleshooting: No rows: workspace or RG placeholder. No stage rows: no orders in the last 24 hours; check the order stream before continuing.
steps.speaker: Freshness is the first cost question: evidence we pay for but do not receive in time answers nothing.
steps.attendee: Know the last arrival time of every evidence source you rely on.

steps.title: Compare with the expected cadence
steps.body: Read AgeMin against ExpectedMaxAgeMin and list what is Stale or silent. Silent sources do not appear at all, so compare with the machine list and the seven expected stages.
steps.code:
$fresh = az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$fresh | Where-Object Freshness -ne 'Fresh' | Format-Table Source, AgeMin, ExpectedMaxAgeMin -AutoSize
$expectedStages = 'Coordinator / Accepted','Transport / Dispatched','OnPremWorker / Started','OnPremWorker / Completed','AwsWorker / Started','AwsWorker / Completed','Coordinator / Completed'
$expectedStages | Where-Object { "Stage / $_" -notin $fresh.Source }
steps.expected: A short list of Stale sources (ideally none) and any silent expected stage. Stages written only on failure (Failed, TimedOut, DeadLettered) are not in the expected list; a silent expected stage is a finding.
steps.troubleshooting: Everything Stale: check the time on the jump and the time range; then check ingestion. Expected ages are presenter settings in the query comments; adjust them to the real order cadence.
steps.speaker: Expected cadence turns a timestamp into a verdict. And a list of what should be there is the only way to see what is missing.
steps.attendee: Write down the expected cadence for each source; without it you cannot call anything stale.

steps.title: Run the billable-volume-by-table query
steps.body: Run the Usage query for the last 30 full days. It shows which tables drive billable ingestion; it is workspace ingestion, not the whole bill.
steps.code:
$q = Get-Content "$S/src/queries/telemetry-volume.kql" -Raw
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: Tables ordered by BillableGB. Guest telemetry (Perf, Syslog) leads; Heartbeat is small; Cas26Service_CL is tiny or absent.
steps.troubleshooting: Empty result: the time range is too short; use a 7-day window. src/fixtures/usage-by-table.jsonl shows the result shape if the query is slow.
steps.speaker: Volume by table is where cost decisions start, because DCRs and table plans are set per stream and per table.
steps.attendee: Start cost work from billable volume by table, not from a guess.

steps.title: Weigh the stage records per order
steps.body: Show what the order evidence costs per order: rows and billed bytes per order from the stage table. This is the evidence that answers 'which stage failed for this customer'.
steps.code:
$q = Get-Content "$S/src/queries/stage-record-volume.kql" -Raw
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: About seven rows per completed order and a small number of bytes per order, split by Environment and DemoTag.
steps.troubleshooting: Division errors or zero orders: no rows with CorrelationId in the last day; check the time range.
steps.speaker: The most valuable evidence in this session is also among the cheapest. Cost reduction should start where volume is high and diagnostic value is low.
steps.attendee: Weigh each table's cost against the question it answers.

steps.title: Name one reduction and the question it would lose
steps.body: Record one decision using the structure from the previous slides: what to reduce, how (DCR filter, sample rate, table plan or retention), the expected saving, and the diagnostic question that would no longer be answerable. Do not apply it on stage.
steps.code:
@"
# M05 decision record ($((Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('u')))
Reduce: <table / stream>
How: <DCR transformation | sample rate | table plan | retention>
Expected saving: <GB per day from the volume query>
Question we would lose: <for example: per-minute CPU during an order failure>
Owner and review date: <name, date>
"@ | Tee-Object -FilePath $S/evidence/local/m05-decision.md
steps.expected: A written record naming one reduction, for example Perf sample interval from 60 to 300 seconds, with the question it loses (minute-level CPU correlation during an order failure) and an owner. The stage records are not the reduction.
steps.troubleshooting: If the volume data is too thin to size a saving, record the decision with the reason and a review date.
steps.speaker: Every reduction removes an answer. Naming the lost question is what makes it a decision instead of a cut.
steps.attendee: Record every telemetry reduction with the diagnostic question it gives up.
